summary:
Maryland stands under United States federal law on identity documents, and that layer is the sharpest document risk for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, so new passports are issued as M or F on the supporting documents submitted, while passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in force since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU is in litigation with the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. An executive order of 5 February 2025 and a State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flag visa applicants with an internal marking, and treat as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

At state level, Maryland's own framework is protective. Gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited statewide since the Fairness for All Marylanders Act took effect 1 October 2014, covering employment, housing and public accommodations; before that, coverage existed only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville and Montgomery County. The hate-crime law adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, with a 2021 amendment effective 1 October 2021 listing gender identity as a separate category, and the common-law gay or trans panic defence was abolished by HB231 effective 1 October 2021.

Maryland declared itself a sanctuary state for protecting and defending transgender individuals by a law passed 33-13 in the Senate and 97-38 in the House, signed by Governor Wes Moore and effective 1 October 2024, following a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and a 1 January 2024 insurance law described as among the most transgender-healthcare-friendly policies in the United States.

Identity documents at state level are comparatively open. Birth-certificate gender-marker change has been allowed since 1 October 2015 without surgery or sterilization, upon certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity, though X remains unavailable on birth certificates as of 2023. Motor Vehicle Administration IDs and voter registration allow X since 1 October 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and the University of Maryland will add X in 2026. Name-change privacy reform HB39 effective 1 October 2021 repealed the 1971 requirement to publish names in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate.

Facilities and sports rules in Maryland favour trans users. A March 2018 federal court ruled that transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms aligning with gender identity, striking down a Talbot County policy; Montgomery County by 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore provide gender-neutral bathrooms by ordinance. A February 2022 county report notes that transgender athletes may participate per gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition, after 2022-2023 bills to restrict teams by biological sex failed.

Care access for residents is expanding. Medicaid explicitly covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18 under a bill passed March 2023, signed April 2023, and effective 1 January 2024. The Trans Health Equity Act passed the Maryland House of Delegates as of 20 May 2024, sponsor Del. Anne Kaiser, D-Montgomery, extending Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment, with its path running through the Maryland Senate. Conversion therapy by licensed practitioners on minors was banned effective 1 October 2018, with a federal constitutional challenge dismissed in September 2019.

Custody remains a documented site of harm nationally, and Maryland has no documented placement rule, special unit, or named case of its own. Federal policy moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018: a January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity; in 2016 the Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy; in 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual to make 'biological sex' the initial determination with gender identity used only 'in rare cases'. Trans women held in men's facilities are subjected to V-coding, the assignment of trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterised as a central part of a trans woman's sentence; trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often criminally charged and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% violent sexual assault, and 88% a 'marriage-like relationship'.

Violence risk persists despite the protective law floor. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died, the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks. A July 2026 analysis plots recorded anti-trans incidents against each state's law score: Maryland sits in the 'Safest States' band (law score 23.5) with 11.1 recorded incidents, while Louisiana tops both worst-laws (24.7) and recorded (11.6) incidents, the piece's point being that protective law floors do not by themselves predict incident counts.

Other federal measures in force or in litigation include the military purge under Executive Order 14183, the women's sports ban under Executive Order 14201, a January 2025 federal funding freeze, and an October 2025 rule blocking student loan forgiveness for public workers who provide gender-affirming care to transgender youth. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.
tangentialFactors:
Maryland's protective statutes do not insulate visitors from federal document and entry rules, which operate at the border and on passport issuance regardless of state law. A trans visitor entering Maryland still presents a federal passport or visa processed under Executive Order 14168.

The July 2026 analysis comparing law scores to incident counts suggests that strong statutory protections coexist with measurable anti-trans violence; Maryland's 11.1 recorded incidents sit close to Louisiana's 11.6 despite the wide gap in law scores.

Baltimore's pattern of killings of Black trans women within a ten-week window in 2026 indicates that lethal violence in the state has been concentrated against a specific demographic, distinct from the general safety picture.

Facilities access in Maryland rests partly on court rulings and county ordinances rather than a single statewide statute, so coverage may vary by locality outside Montgomery County and Baltimore.

The Trans Health Equity Act's progress through the House with Senate action pending means Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming treatment for residents may still be subject to legislative change.

No Maryland-specific data on transgender prisoners in state custody, or on V-coding incidence within Maryland facilities, is available in these sources; the V-coding and 2021 California study findings are national or out-of-state evidence.
